explanation: Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and handle more escape sequences, while single-quoted strings are processed literally (except \ ' ).
The null coalescing operator (??) uses isset-like semantics, so it returns the right-hand operand when the left is null or undefined without emitting any warning.
The echo construct can take multiple arguments and prints them concatenated without any separator.
print is an expression in PHP that outputs text and returns the integer 1, so it can be used inside expressions like $x = print 'hi';
The elvis operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, and evaluates and returns the right operand when the left one is falsy.
In PHP 8.0 the concatenation operator (.) was changed to have the same precedence as the arithmetic operators + and -, not lower.
PHP's ** operator is right-associative, so it evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
`.` and `+` have the same precedence and are left-associative, so it evaluates as (`'sum: ' . 2`) + 3 = "sum: 2" + 3, and the non-numeric string converts to 0, giving 3.
In PHP, the === operator for arrays requires the same key/value pairs in the same order with the same types, so element order does matter.
`==` is a loose comparison, and 0 == false evaluates to true in PHP, so both parts of the statement are wrong.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string with a number casts the number to a string instead, so "abc" == 0 compares "abc" with "0" and is false.
With == (loose comparison), null is equal to 0, empty string, and false, so all three comparisons return true.
Casting the string '42abc' to int stops at the first non-numeric character, yielding 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer for arithmetic addition, so '5' + 5 equals 10.
In PHP, casting false to string yields an empty string "", not "0"; only (int)false gives 0.
0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004 in IEEE 754 floating point arithmetic, so it does not exactly equal 0.3.
strrev() operates on bytes, not characters, so it can break multibyte UTF-8 sequences (use a multibyte-safe approach instead).
str_contains() checks if the substring 'world' exists within 'Hello world', which it does, so it returns true.
str_pad() can pad on the left, right, or both sides using the $pad_type parameter (STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default trim() strips spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, NUL bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' occupies 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 1+2+1+1+1 = 6.
substr with a negative start returns the substring from that offset to the end, so the last 3 characters are returned.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character converted to uppercase; it does not modify the original, as PHP strings are passed by value.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) parses variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') treats content as a literal single-quoted string.
sort() reindexes numeric keys, discarding the original key-to-value association (use asort() to preserve it).
PHP casts array keys that are canonical integer strings (like '5') to integers automatically.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default unless the third $strict parameter is set to true.
Without a callback, array_filter() removes elements that evaluate to false, including 0, '', null, false, and [].
By default, array_slice() reindexes numeric keys unless the preserve_keys parameter is set to true.
array_slice returns elements starting at index 1 with a length of 2, so it yields 20 and 30.
The + union operator keeps values from the left array for duplicate keys, so 'a' stays 1 and 'b' is added, giving 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for string keys in array unpacking, so [...] merges string-keyed arrays like array_merge.
PHP allows mixing them (e.g. foo(...$args, a: 1, b: 2), and since 8.1 also foo(a: 1, ...$args) with string keys) — only a positional argument after a named one is forbidden.
Anonymous functions only get access to outer scope variables when they are explicitly imported with the use keyword.
func_num_args() returns the total number of arguments actually passed to the function, which is 3 despite only one parameter being declared.
In PHP, an arrow function declared with fn must contain exactly one expression as its body and cannot use a curly-brace block (that syntax belongs to regular closures/function() {}).
PHP arrow functions capture outer variables by value at creation time (like `use ($x)`), not by reference read lazily at call time — only object handles are shared.
A static closure cannot bind $this, so it captures neither $this nor any auto-bound context, though it can still capture variables by use.
The closure captures $x by value at definition time, so it still holds 5 even after $x is reassigned to 7.
Without strict_types, PHP performs type juggling and converts the numeric string "5" to the integer 5 instead of throwing a TypeError.
PHP 8.0 introduced constructor property promotion, allowing visibility modifiers and types directly in __construct parameters.
The `final` keyword prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses.
The final modifier prevents child classes from overriding or reimplementing the method.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that declares them, not in subclasses.
Anonymous classes get the name 'class@anonymous' plus a NUL byte followed by the file path, line and counter, so the part before the NUL is 'class@anonymous'.
Private parent methods are excluded from inheritance, so a child can redefine the same name with any visibility without a compatibility fatal error.
__get() is called both for non-existent properties and for existing but inaccessible (private/protected) properties.
In PHP, attempting to modify a readonly property throws an Error, not an Exception.
PHP interfaces may declare public constants (since PHP 7.1 constants may have visibility, and they have always been allowed as implicitly public).
The instanceof operator returns true if the object is an instance of the given class or implements the given interface.
Since PHP 8.0, interfaces can declare static methods that implementing classes must define as static.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a class (including its parent classes) or implements an interface.
PHP interfaces cannot provide method bodies; only traits and (abstract) classes can supply default implementations.
Abstract methods may be declared with public or protected visibility (private is not allowed), so protected is valid.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all cases of the enum, and this enum declares three cases (A, B, and C).
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, though before that version they could not.
In PHP 7+, both the Exception and Error classes implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error (from the Throwable hierarchy), not Exception, so it will not be caught by catch (Exception $e).
The @ operator only suppresses error/warning/notices, not exceptions.
intdiv() throws a DivisionByZeroError when the divisor is zero, unlike the modulo operator which throws ArithmeticError.
The finally block executes whether or not an exception is caught, including when no exception occurs at all.
An exception thrown in a finally block replaces any exception or return value from the try block, discarding it.
Objects are always truthy in PHP, so casting an Exception to bool yields true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() execute when exit() or die() is called, as the script is ending.
The use statement only imports the class name as an alias; the file is loaded lazily by the autoloader when the class is actually first referenced.
In PHP, the `use function` syntax imports a function, whereas `use const` is used to import a constant.
PSR-4 strips the App\ prefix mapped to src/ and appends the remaining namespace path plus the class name with a .php extension.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php registers its class-loading mechanism using spl_autoload_register().
The magic constant __NAMESPACE__ is a case-insensitive pre-defined constant that returns the name of the current namespace (an empty string if none is used).
Unqualified class names in `new` are resolved relative to the current namespace (with a fallback to the global namespace), not directly from the root.
PSR-4 strips the mapped prefix App\ and appends the remaining sub-namespace and class name to src/, yielding src/Model/User.php.
PHP requires import (use) statements to be in the outermost scope of a file, so placing one inside a function body triggers a fatal compile error rather than a function-scoped alias.
In PHP, arrays are assigned by value using copy-on-write unless explicitly assigned by reference with the & operator.
PHP arrays are copied by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, leaving it with 2 elements.
In PHP, variables defined outside a function are local to it by default, so you must use the global keyword, $GLOBALS array, or pass them as parameters to access them.
$GLOBALS['x'] refers to the actual global symbol table entry, so unset removes it everywhere, not just locally to the function.
The function takes $n by reference, so $x++ modifies $n itself from 5 to 6.
foreach by value iterates over a copy (copy-on-write separation), so writes to the array during the loop are not seen in the current pass.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances, so changes are visible to every object.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers: true becomes 1 and false becomes 0, so keys are never stored as bool.
Since PHP 7.0, a generator can `return` a value which is then retrievable via `$gen->getReturn()` after the generator has finished.
Calling rewind() on a generator that has already run (i.e., fully consumed) throws an Exception, so it cannot be traversed again.
The yield from expression iterates over the given iterable (including generators), forwarding values bidirectionally with send() and returning the sub-generator's return value.
Calling a function containing yield returns a Generator object, whose class name is Generator.
The generator yields three values (1, 2, 3) via yield from, so iterator_to_array produces an array with 3 elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO (last-in, first-out) stack, not a FIFO queue; that role belongs to SplQueue.
ArrayIterator wraps an array (or object) and implements the Iterator interface, allowing foreach traversal.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
Since PHP 7.0 (and the salt parameter was deprecated in 7.4 and removed in 8.0), password_hash() automatically generates a cryptographically random salt, so providing one separately is unnecessary.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is bcrypt (CRYPT_BLOWFISH) with an automatically generated salt, not md5.
password_verify correctly matches the plain password against the generated hash, returning true.
strip_tags() only removes HTML tags; SQL injection must be prevented with prepared statements or proper escaping.
session_regenerate_id() generates a new session ID, helping prevent attackers from fixing a known session ID on a victim before login.
The built-in function php_sapi_name() returns the SAPI interface name, such as 'cli'.
session_destroy() only removes the session data stored on the server; the session cookie remains in the browser until it expires or is explicitly removed with setcookie() or session_unset().
session_start() must be called before $_SESSION is populated with session data.
The array_find() function, along with array_find_key(), array_any(), and array_all(), was added in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get and set logic to be defined directly in a property's declaration.
PHP 8.4 introduced the asymmetric visibility RFC, allowing different read/write visibility such as `public private(set)`.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which flags functions whose return values must not be ignored, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5 as a way to pass the result of an expression as the first argument to the next call.
The clone-with syntax (clone($obj, ['x' => 1])) was introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.5.
array_first() and array_last() are not native PHP functions, so they were never introduced in any PHP version.
The Partial Function Application RFC (v2) was accepted for inclusion in PHP 8.5.
The clamp_v2 RFC was accepted and its clamp() function was implemented in the PHP 8.6 release line.
Context Managers v2 has not been adopted in PHP; no such RFC is part of the language as of that date.
No PHP RFC named "Bound-Erased Generic Types" exists, so it could not have been declined in 2026.
No RFC making ZTS the default build has been accepted as of that date; it remains a non-default configure option (only discussed/planned for future versions).
PHP still has no native support for generics or parameterized types, even in version 8.5.
PHP 8.5 was released on November 20, 2025, making it the latest stable version on 2026-11-07, while PHP 8.6's general availability is still upcoming in November 2026.
The planned PHP 6 with native Unicode support was cancelled, so PHP 7.0 directly followed PHP 5.6.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute RFC was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4, allowing functions, methods, and properties to be marked as deprecated so calling/using them raises a deprecation notice.
Both Clean and Onion Architecture impose the Dependency Rule: source code dependencies only point inward, so inner (domain) layers never reference outer (infrastructure/UI) ones.
Domain entities should be framework-agnostic, depending only on the language and standard library to keep the domain layer pure.
Controllers handle HTTP request/response and Twig templates render views, while business logic lives in use cases/services/entities.
In the onion architecture, the innermost layer contains the domain model (entities/business rules), which has no dependencies on outer layers.
Tools like deptrac statically analyse class dependencies against configured layer rules and report (and fail on) any forbidden cross-layer call, making boundary violations a CI-failing event.
In Clean Architecture, use cases must depend only on abstractions (ports), not on framework-specific details like HTTP request objects or an ORM's EntityManager.
A repository provides a collection-like interface for accessing aggregates/entities while abstracting away the underlying persistence mechanism.
In clean architecture, database details live in the infrastructure/outer layer behind interfaces, so replacing PostgreSQL leaves the domain and use case layers untouched.
An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data consistency, not a database table.
In Domain-Driven Design, value objects are immutable and have no identity, so equality is determined by comparing their attribute values.
In Domain-Driven Design, all external access to an aggregate's members is restricted to its single entry-point entity, the aggregate root.
In DDD, repositories provide access to whole aggregates by their root, so individual entities inside an aggregate are not given their own repositories.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is a common, shared vocabulary for the model used consistently by both developers and domain experts.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary inside which a model and its ubiquitous language remain consistent, while outside the same terms may mean different things in other contexts.
DDD recommends a rich domain model where objects encapsulate behavior and invariants, not anemic models with logic pushed to services.
In DDD, each bounded context owns its own domain model, so an identical concept (e.g., Product) is modeled as a distinct class in each context.
Symfony instantiates a service only when it is first requested from the container, along with its dependencies.
The `debug:router` Symfony console command lists all registered routes along with their methods, URIs, and defaults.
Autowiring automatically resolves constructor type-hints without needing explicit service definitions in services.yaml.
Twig compiles templates into optimized PHP classes and caches them to avoid recompilation between requests.
In dev the kernel only performs a freshness check on each request (comparing mtimes of tracked resources), so the container is actually recompiled only when one of those files changes.
The APP_ENV environment variable tells Symfony which environment (dev, prod, test, etc.) to run, defaulting to dev.
Symfony's controller resolver only invokes public methods, so a private controller method cannot be routed to.
Implementing EventSubscriberInterface grants no priority — ordering depends on explicit priority values in getSubscribedEvents() or on how/when listeners are registered.
Symfony 6.0 removed the legacy guard authentication system and standardized on AuthenticatorInterface-based authenticators.
The IsGranted attribute (e.g. #[IsGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')]) denies access with a 403 unless the user has the given role/permission.
In Symfony's Security component, voters (implementing the VoterInterface) are consulted by the authorization checker's isGranted method to determine access to a given object and attribute.
In Symfony 7+, validation constraints use PHP 8 attributes and Doctrine annotation support was removed (deprecated in 6.4).
Symfony forms enable CSRF protection by default with a token that is validated on submission.
Symfony forms are always validated on the server side, regardless of any HTML5 client-side validation.
The Symfony MakerBundle command 'make:form' interactively generates a new FormType class.
Symfony stores only minimal user identifiers (like the username and roles) in the session, never the password, so it is reloaded from the database on each request.

In the standard Symfony structure, each bundle or topic gets its own configuration file under config/packages (e.g., framework.yaml, twig.yaml), though configuration can also be split elsewhere if desired.
This is a common practice where the committed .env holds only development defaults while .env.local (git-ignored) stores the real secrets.
The debug:container command lists all registered services (and with --alias, their aliases) in the dependency injection container.
setParameter() only exists on ContainerBuilder before compilation; the compiled container used at runtime has no setParameter() method and its parameter bag is frozen/read-only.
Since Symfony 3.4/4.0, services are private by default and must be explicitly marked as public to be fetched directly from the container.
Bundles typically provide sensible default configuration and can work without any config file being present.
Symfony uses the %env(VAR)% placeholder syntax in configuration files like services.yaml to reference environment variables.
The APP_DEBUG environment variable controls whether debug mode is enabled, activating the profiler and Twig debugging.
A single message can be handled by multiple handlers, each receiving a copy of it.
The sync transport sends the message back to the bus immediately in the same process instead of queuing it for an async worker.
In Symfony, the 'messenger:consume' console command starts a worker that processes messages from the Messenger transport queues.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy options are set under each transport's configuration (messenger.transports.<name>.retry_strategy), so retries are defined per transport rather than globally.
Symfony Messenger's default transport serializer encodes the message envelope to JSON.
Symfony Scheduler registers recurrent messages and dispatches them through the Messenger component at scheduled times.
Symfony Messenger ships a Doctrine transport that queues messages in database tables using a Doctrine connection.
Symfony's Messenger component lets you configure custom middleware and position them relative to built-in ones in the bus stack.
Symfony's release policy schedules new major versions every two years (e.g., 4.0 in Nov 2017, 5.0 in Nov 2019, 6.0 in Nov 2021) and minor versions every six months, in May and November.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.4 or higher as its minimum supported PHP version.
Symfony 7.0 removed Doctrine docblock annotation support, requiring PHP 8 attributes instead.
Symfony's AssetMapper imports JavaScript/CSS assets using an importmap.php file, requiring neither Node.js nor Webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release, receiving three years of maintenance support.
Symfony removes deprecated features in the next major release; deprecations are only kept working until that major version.
Symfony provides UPGRADE-*.md files (e.g., UPGRADE-4.0.md, UPGRADE-5.0.md) detailing BC-breaking changes for each major release.
Symfony's AssetMapper component compiles and serves assets (JS/CSS) and manages the importmap.json without requiring Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 would not be released until late November 2026, after the 2026-11-07 date.
Following the six-month cycle after 8.0 (Nov 2025) and 8.1 (May 2026), Symfony 8.2 lands in November 2026.
Symfony's minor versions are released every six months, so 8.1 (May 2026) is followed by 8.2 in November 2026.
Symfony follows semantic versioning, so 8.2 would be a minor (backward-compatible) release, not a major one requiring rewrites.
PHP's backward compatibility promise guarantees that code running on 8.1 keeps working on 8.2, since minor releases within a major version only add features and deprecate, never remove.
Symfony 8.4 (LTS) is the final minor release of the 8.x branch, arriving in November 2027 right before Symfony 9.0.
Symfony only raises the minimum PHP version at major releases, so Symfony 8.x would still target PHP 8.4 rather than PHP 8.5.
Symfony's policy states that deprecations introduced in 8.x are only removed in the next major version, 9.0.
Twig's {{ }} only evaluates Twig expressions, functions, and filters — it cannot execute arbitrary PHP code directly.
Twig enables HTML auto-escaping by default, so variables printed with {{ }} are escaped unless |raw is used or autoescape is disabled.
The Twig |e filter (escape) by default escapes characters for safe HTML output, with optional strategy arguments like 'js', 'css', 'url', or 'html_attr'.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number using IntlNumberFormatter according to a given locale.
The |raw filter in Twig marks a value as safe HTML, disabling the auto-escaping that would otherwise be applied on output.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs an expression's value, while {% %} denotes tags like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables with the {% set %} tag inside templates.
The dump() function outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to var_dump in PHP.
Bootstrap is a front-end framework of prebuilt UI components and is not itself an SPA framework.
The .container class applies a fixed max-width at each responsive breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always full width.
The Bootstrap grid is indeed based on CSS floats, but it divides a row into 12 columns, not 16.
Bootstrap 5 defines five responsive infixes — sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl — corresponding to its named breakpoints.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities multiply $spacer by the scale number, so .mt-3 is margin-top: $spacer * 3.
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to activate interactive components via JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and its components are implemented in plain vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode via the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not create tables automatically; schema must be created beforehand using the SchemaTool, doctrine:schema:create, or migrations.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity as managed in the identity map, deferring any INSERT SQL until flush() is called.
EntityManager::merge() was removed in Doctrine ORM 3, so it no longer exists to make objects managed.
DQL is Doctrine's object-oriented query language that operates on entities and their fields rather than underlying database tables and columns.
Doctrine's Repository::find() returns null when no entity matching the given identifier is found.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically flush; you must call flush() explicitly on the EntityManager.
Managed entities are tracked by the Unit of Work, so changes are detected and written on flush() without calling persist().
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only marks the entity for deletion; the DELETE statement is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC allows readers and writers to proceed concurrently without blocking each other; readers see a snapshot and writers work on new versions.
The EXPLAIN command displays the query execution plan without running the query.

SERIAL is only shorthand that creates a sequence and a DEFAULT nextval(), while GENERATED AS IDENTITY is a standard-conforming column-level feature with stricter control (e.g., GENERATED ALWAYS forbids manual inserts), so they are not identical mechanisms.
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct in UNIQUE constraints, so multiple rows with NULL are allowed by default.
string_agg() is the PostgreSQL aggregate function that concatenates string values into one, separated by a specified delimiter.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead-tuple space as reusable for future rows; only VACUUM FULL (which rewrites the table) returns space to the operating system.
The PARTITION BY clause divides the result set into groups (partitions) over which the window function is evaluated.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; it still allows non-repeatable reads, which require REPEATABLE READ (or higher) to prevent.
Outside an explicit BEGIN block, PostgreSQL executes each statement in its own implicitly started and auto-committed transaction, which is autocommit behavior.
COMMIT ends the current transaction and permanently saves all changes made within it.
UPDATE and DELETE statements with WHERE clauses on indexed columns use the index to locate rows faster, just like SELECT does.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to define points within a transaction to which you can roll back with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, undoing only part of the transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query (unlike plain EXPLAIN) and reports actual runtime statistics such as real row counts and elapsed time.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that adds the vector data type and supports HNSW/IVFFlat indexes for efficient embedding similarity search.
A partial index only indexes rows that satisfy the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster for queries matching that condition.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects read-write dependencies via predicate locks rather than locking rows.
HTTP status code 201 is defined as 'Created', indicating that the request has been fulfilled and a new resource has been created as a result.
204 No Content indicates the request succeeded but there is no content to return in the response body.
HTTP defines DELETE as idempotent, meaning repeated deletion of the same resource leaves the server in the same state as a single deletion.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header is sent by the server (in response to a preflight or CORS request) to indicate which origins are allowed, not by the client.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests is specifically defined for situations where a client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, exceeding a rate limit.
4xx codes indicate client-side errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the media type (MIME type) of the resource in the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas PUT must be.
Using == is vulnerable to timing attacks; you should use hash_equals() for constant-time comparison.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, tied to the user's session, and validated on unsafe requests to prevent cross-site request forgery.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header is used to enable and configure CSP for a page.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework; an access token grants permissions (scopes), and identifying the user requires an ID token (OpenID Connect) or a separate resource call.
XSS is prevented by context-aware output encoding/escaping when rendering, since input validation alone cannot cover all injection paths (e.g., data from other sources or contexts).
The authorization code is returned to the redirect_uri and then exchanged for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens are designed with longer lifetimes than access tokens and are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
A salt is stored with the hash and need not be secret; it only prevents rainbow table attacks and makes each hash unique, so verification still works without keeping it hidden.
PHPUnit only discovers and runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase.
setUp() runs before each individual test method, while setUpBeforeClass() is the static method that runs once before all tests in the class.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, so the test runs once for each set.
The expectException($exceptionClass) method sets an expectation that the code under test will throw an exception of the specified class.
It's the reverse: stubs provide canned return values while mocks record and verify interactions with methods.
PHPUnit 10 introduced PHP attributes like #[DataProvider] as the preferred approach and deprecated doc-comment annotations, which were removed in PHPUnit 11.
PHPUnit supports the @depends annotation, which explicitly lets one test depend on the result of another.
The --order-by=random option randomizes test execution order in PHPUnit.
